author: fwyzard
body: **This is a draft PR, opened as a request for comments: it is not meant to be merged in its current form.** #### PR description: On machines with more than one NUMA node, a single job using all the cpus is slower than the same cpus split among one job per socket: the threads of a stream migrate between nodes, and the stream's data and the EventSetup products are read from remote memory. This PR adds `process.options.numaLocality` (default `False`). When it is enabled and the job's cpus span more than one NUMA node, it: - creates one TBB arena per NUMA domain, and assigns the framework threads, including the main thread, to the arenas in proportion to the number of cpus (hardware threads) available to the job in each domain; the threads of each arena are pinned to the cpus of its domain; the main thread joins the first arena in a slot reserved for it and, while it waits for the transitions, runs any task of that arena like the other threads; - assigns the streams to the NUMA domains in the same proportion, in contiguous blocks, and runs each event in the arena of its stream's domain; all the tasks spawned by the event stay in that arena; - starts each event through `numa::runInDomain()`: on the local queue of the reading thread if it already runs in the arena of the event's stream, otherwise in the queue of that arena; - constructs the per-stream objects (stream schedules, workers, event principals) on the node of their stream; - gives each domain its own copy of the EventSetup products, produced by a task running in the arena of that domain; `process.options.eventSetup.numaReplicatedRecords` and `numaExcludedRecords` restrict the replication to, or exclude from it, some records; - sets a local memory policy for the whole job (as `numactl --localalloc`), from `cmsRun` and `PythonEventProcessor` before the TBB worker threads are created; this also takes the job out of the kernel's automatic NUMA balancing; - makes the FastTimerService observe the per-domain arenas, so that their threads are registered and timed. It also warns about jobs that are not pinned and have fewer threads than cpus, and reports at the end of the job how many threads moved between arenas. Nothing changes if `numaLocality` is not enabled; if the job's cpus are all on one NUMA node, only the memory policy applies. #### Open points for discussion 1. **One option or one per feature.** `numaLocality` enables everything together. The pieces could be controlled separately instead, e.g. `process.options.numa = cms.untracked.PSet(arenas = ..., streamPlacement = ..., replicateEventSetup = ..., memoryPolicy = ...)`. 2. **Setting the memory policy in the code.** The same policy can be set from outside the job with `numactl --localalloc`; this PR sets it in `cmsRun` and `PythonEventProcessor` when `numaLocality` is enabled. The impact on a "sane" machine is also very small, but it was observed to be very significant on a machine with a higher cost for the memory transfers across sockets. 3. The comment ```c++ // TBB's own NUMA binding (tbbbind) does not take effect inside a restricted cpuset, so pin the threads explicitly ``` is incorrect, and we _can_ use TBB NUMA support. However the code is not much simpler, because we need to map cores from the kernel numbering to the hwloc numbering. #### Known issues with the EventSetup implementation - EventSetup products are _produced_ N times, one per NUMA domain. At least some of them could be produced _once_ on one NUMA domain and copied to the other domains: this may require a way to distinguish which ES products are safe to copy and which ones are not. - The N copies cost additional memory. In the HLT test, it was measured to about 0.56 GB per additional NUMA domain. In the context of a 90-core jobs this is probably negligible. - The N copies may have side effects, going from trivial (like log messages) to problematic (incorrectly shared resources, creation of external files, etc.). - The N copies may lead to a significant slowdown in the startup time and acriss IOV boundaries. - The `PoolDBESSource` (aka the GlobalTag) downloads and decompresses N copies of the payloads, one per NUMA domain. This is clearly not optimal and should be improved. - alpaka ESProducers create NM copies of their payloads in GPU memory (number of NUMA domains times the number of GPUs). A first fix is to make them create only one copy. A possible improvement would be to fill each GPU's single payload from a task running on the closest NUMA domain. Longer term the assignment of the streams, GPUs and NUMA domains needs to be investigated and improved significantly. - With EventSetup replication, `ESProductResolverProvider::initConcurrentIOVs()` receives the number of concurrent IOVs multiplied by the number of domains; producers that size per-IOV caches by it see the larger number. In general, the interplay between stream modules and NUMA domains should be revisited. #### Other known points - The main thread reads the source, runs the global transitions and produces the non-replicated EventSetup products inside the first arena, so the first NUMA domain carries some more work than its share of streams. I don't think anything can be done about the global transitions. In the future the source (or at least some types of source) could maybe be made aware of the NUMA domains. - The FastTimerService finds the per-domain arenas through `edm::numa::StreamNumaDomains`, so `HLTrigger/Timer` now depends on `FWCore/Concurrency`. The arenas are created before the `preallocate` signal is emitted, so they could be passed to the services with it, through `SystemBounds`, which would remove that dependency. #### Measurements Run 3 HLT menu `/online/collisions/2026/2e34/v1.3/HLT/V2`, run 402360 HLTPhysics data read with `DAQSource`, CPU only, jobs pinned with `taskset`, threads = streams = cpus including SMT. Raw throughput in events per second, average sigma. All measurements include the service rework of #52158; this PR is compared with #52158 alone, with `numaLocality` enabled, with and without the local memory policy. On a 2 AMD EPYC 9655 (2 96 cores, 190 usable), `CMSSW_20_1_X_2026-10-23-1100` with the release's jemalloc, 4 repetitions: | configuration | #52158 | + this PR without the memory policy | | + this PR | | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | one job, 190 cores | 771.7 2.7 | 812.7 4.4 | +5.3% 0.7% | 816.4 3.0 | +5.8% 0.5% | | two jobs, one per socket | 845.6 1.2 | 843.4 1.1 | 0.3% 0.2% | 844.2 0.5 | 0.2% 0.2% | | 24 jobs, one per CCD | 871.6 0.2 | 870.6 0.1 | 0.1% 0.1% | 870.8 0.3 | 0.1% 0.1% | The single job reaches 91.3% 0.3% of the two per-socket jobs with #52158 alone, 96.4% 0.5% with this PR without the memory policy, and 96.7% 0.4% with it. When each job stays within one socket or one CCD nothing changes, as expected. In the single job, the share of the DRAM fills that come from the other socket (`perf stat`, user space, one run each) goes from 40.5% with #52158 alone to 13.0% with this PR without the memory policy and 16.8% with it, while the number of DRAM fills per instruction stays the same (0.38-0.39 per 1000 instructions); with one job per socket or per CCD it is 0.2-0.3% in all cases. Scaling with the number of cores (cores added in order, socket 0 first, 4 repetitions, shaded band = sigma), and the same throughput divided by the IB extrapolated linearly from one CCD: At a fixed clock (3.0 GHz, the clock of the full machine) the three versions follow the extrapolation from one CCD up to about 80 cores. On the second socket #52158 alone falls to 88-93% of it, while with this PR it stays at 93-96%; on the full machine 90.3% 0.3% with #52158 alone, 92.8% 0.6% and 93.2% 0.8% with this PR without and with the memory policy. #### PR validation: Unit tests of FWCore/Concurrency, FWCore/ServiceRegistry, FWCore/Framework, FWCore/ParameterSet, FWCore/PythonFramework, FWCore/TestProcessor and HLTrigger/Timer pass. The HLT throughput measurements above ran with `numaLocality` enabled on the 2 EPYC 9655; with it disabled the framework behaves as before.
title: [RFC] Keep the work and data of each stream on one NUMA node
